[📥 Download the R script](two_way_anova.R){.btn .btn-primary download="two_way_anova.R"}

The data come from the `palmerpenguins` package, so there is no file to download. Run `install.packages("palmerpenguins")` once if you need it.

## What two-way ANOVA does

Two-way ANOVA tests two categorical factors at once, **and** whether they interact:

$$Y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}$$

It tests three null hypotheses:

1. **Factor A** (species): no difference among species means.
2. **Factor B** (sex): no difference between sexes.
3. **Interaction A × B**: the effect of sex is the **same** in every species.

**Check the interaction first.** If it is significant, the main effects are averages over situations that differ, so you should compare one factor *within* each level of the other (simple effects).

**Data:** body mass of three penguin species, by sex.

## Step 1: Load packages and data

```{r}
#| label: step-1-load
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(car)              # Anova(), leveneTest()
library(emmeans)          # marginal means and post-hoc tests
library(palmerpenguins)   # the data

p_df <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(sex), !is.na(species)) %>%
  select(species, sex, body_mass_g)

count(p_df, species, sex)
```

## Step 2: Balance the design

The cells have unequal n. As in lecture, we first sample the same number from every cell so the three types of sums of squares agree. (Step 9 shows what changes when the data are unbalanced.)

```{r}
#| label: step-2-balance
min_n <- min(count(p_df, species, sex)$n)

set.seed(123)
balanced_df <- p_df %>%
  group_by(species, sex) %>%
  slice_sample(n = min_n) %>%
  ungroup()

count(balanced_df, species, sex)
```

## Step 3: Summarize and plot

```{r}
#| label: step-3-summary
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3
balanced_df %>%
  group_by(species, sex) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
            mean = mean(body_mass_g),
            se = sd(body_mass_g) / sqrt(n),
            .groups = "drop")

balanced_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(species, body_mass_g, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Step 4: Fit the model with sum-to-zero contrasts

Type III tests are only correct with **sum-to-zero contrasts**. Set them before fitting.

```{r}
#| label: step-4-fit
options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))

anova_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species * sex, data = balanced_df)
```

`species * sex` is shorthand for `species + sex + species:sex`.

## Step 5: Check the assumptions

```{r}
#| label: step-5-assumptions
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(anova_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

shapiro.test(residuals(anova_model))
leveneTest(body_mass_g ~ species * sex, data = balanced_df)
```

## Step 6: The ANOVA table

```{r}
#| label: step-6-anova
anova_type3 <- Anova(anova_model, type = "III")
anova_type3
```

Read it **bottom up**: the `species:sex` interaction is significant, so the size of the sex difference depends on species. The main-effect rows are still true, but they are averages.

## Step 7: Follow up the interaction

The six **cell** means, then species compared **within each sex** (simple effects):

```{r}
#| label: step-7-emmeans
interaction_emm <- emmeans(anova_model, ~ species * sex)
interaction_emm

# F-test for species within each sex
joint_tests(anova_model, by = "sex")

# Tukey pairwise comparisons of species within each sex
pairs(interaction_emm, by = "sex", adjust = "tukey")
```

Compact letter display for all six cells (cells sharing a letter do not differ):

```{r}
#| label: step-7b-cld
multcomp::cld(interaction_emm, Letters = letters, adjust = "sidak")
```

## Step 8: Interaction plot

Non-parallel lines are what an interaction looks like.

```{r}
#| label: step-8-plot
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3
emm_df <- as.data.frame(interaction_emm)

emm_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(species, emmean, color = sex, group = sex)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = emmean - SE, ymax = emmean + SE), width = 0.1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean body mass (g) ± SE", color = "Sex") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Step 9: Unbalanced data — why Type III

With unequal cell sizes, Type I (sequential) sums of squares change with the **order** of the terms; Type II and III do not. Compare on the full, unbalanced data:

```{r}
#| label: step-9-unbalanced
unbal_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species * sex, data = p_df)

anova(unbal_model)                 # Type I: order matters
Anova(unbal_model, type = "III")   # Type III: use this with an interaction

# put R's default contrasts back when you are done
options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))
```

## Step 10: Write it up

> Body mass differed among species (F~2,198~ = `r round(anova_type3["species", "F value"], 1)`, p < 0.001) and between sexes (F~1,198~ = `r round(anova_type3["sex", "F value"], 1)`, p < 0.001), and the sex difference depended on species (species × sex interaction: F~2,198~ = `r round(anova_type3["species:sex", "F value"], 1)`, p < 0.001; two-way ANOVA, Type III SS). Males were heavier than females in all three species, with the largest difference in Gentoo penguins.

Report all three F-tests with df and p, then describe the interaction using the cell means and the interaction plot.
